scope: Read-only 64 sampled changed code positions from full10M comparison. Raw vectors read from documented first-million prefix of same YFCC10M source; root may independently verify sample vector hashes. No runtime source edits.
rust_kernel_model: Float32 folded absolute pivots; six-dimensional square-norm SIMD reduction matching x86-64-v3; sequential float32 FMA dot; norm-minus-two-dot; equal-score reduction by SIMD lane then code.
conclusion: All 64 sampled Rust assignments are reproduced exactly by a scalar float32 model of the existing x86-64-v3 encoder. Selected true f64 centroid errors differ by at most 0.0192067 squared-L2 (maximum relative gap 0.00463188%). Together with identical headers, sparse uniformly distributed full-file changes, and independently verified source vectors, this supports near-boundary float32 encoding differences rather than row/chunk remapping or a serialization defect. This sample does not prove every one of the 6,175 changed positions, and small point reconstruction-error differences do not bound ADC distance or ANN recall differences for arbitrary queries.
corrective_plan: Keep runtime/source unchanged while root performs same-native-graph original-C++-code quality ablation. Existing native result logs remain valid observations; no code-byte parity or isolated graph-only claim.
Frozen codebook reuse preserves the trained quantizer asset, not an exact cross-language compressed-code contract. Document this distinction and retain full-code comparison evidence.

If bitwise migration compatibility becomes a product requirement, validate/import original compressed codes for immutable migrated rows or add a separately tested legacy encoding mode reproducing centering, BLAS norm/dot arithmetic and centroid tie order. Centering alone cannot guarantee BLAS byte parity.

source_mechanisms.behavior: Rust adds the saved nonzero centroid to each residual pivot, rounding to absolute float32 pivots.
Rust computes direct float32 pivot norms and sequential SIMD FMA dots, omits common query norm, and reduces equal scores by SIMD lane order.
C++ subtracts the centroid from each input coordinate before nearest-center compression.
C++ norms use BLAS snrm2 then square; BLAS SGEMM forms queryNorm+centerNorm-2dot, and ascending centroid IDs break exact score ties.
